article.articleSummary:
- DRC Ebola outbreak has exceeded 6,000 confirmed cases and 2,911 deaths (case fatality 48.2%) as of August 31, more than 100 days since the May 15 start. WHO cautions the outbreak could become the deadliest in history, with actual infections potentially three times the confirmed tally. The Bundibugyo ebolavirus strain is implicated; forest origin confirmed by sequencing, though there is no targeted vaccine or therapy for this strain. Ituri Province remains the epicenter in a mining region with high cross-border movement, complicating surveillance and care, and about six to seven deaths occur outside treatment centers. - As of 2 September 2026, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached 6,100 confirmed cases, with 2,950 deaths and 1,383 recoveries. Kisangani city in central DRC is among affected areas, indicating spread from the eastern outbreak that began mid-May. Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for about 82.3% of total infections, with 44 of 59 new cases in Ituri in the last 24 hours and 15 of 20 deaths also in Ituri. Overall 814 people are isolated or hospitalized; contact tracing is 86.3% complete. Six provinces are affected: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele, and Bas-Uele, triggering international alerts due to the widening reach and concerns about outbreak response capacity.
- Britain will provide more than £50 million (about $67.6 million) to help contain the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, bringing its total contribution to £78 million (from £20m initial allocation in May). The funds will support disease surveillance, frontline health workers, access to treatment, infection prevention and control, community outreach, and safe burials. UK public health experts have been deployed to Congo. African Affairs Minister Kirsty McNeill said the response will accelerate to match the scale of the challenge. The outbreak, driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain, is the second-largest and fastest-spreading on record, with confirmed cases exceeding 6,000; there are no approved vaccines or treatments for this strain.

In the last 24 hours, 59 new cases and 39 deaths were reported, with 17 recoveries. Ten countries in East, Central, and Southern Africa have tightened border health checks to curb cross-border transmission. There is no vaccine or treatment formally approved for Bundibugyo ebolavirus, the strain involved, though laboratory data indicate that the Ervebo vaccine—distributed from the global Ebola vaccine stockpile to Congo—may offer some protection. The situation signals ongoing escalation and heightened regional surveillance as authorities pursue containment amid international concern.

The article notes hot-water rinsing may reduce but not eliminate bacteria, with effectiveness varying by temperature and duration.

article.articleHeadline: Girl develops over 20 "pearly papules" all over her body after swimming for more than 20 days; doctors warn: pools are high-risk transmission zones—don't squeeze, or it will spread.
article.articleSummary: Henan Province, China reports a molluscum contagiosum case in a girl after more than 20 days of swimming in summer, who developed over 20 pearly, waxy, dome-shaped papules with a central tiny navellike indentation all over her body. Lesions are usually painless but can spread via scratching; squeezing can eject white curd-like material containing active virus, greatly increasing transmission. Transmission occurs through direct skin contact, contact with contaminated items (towels, swim gear), or autoinoculation to other body parts. Pools in summer are high-risk zones since the virus can survive in moist, warm environments and is hard to eliminate with standard chlorine. Prevention emphasizes skin-barrier protection and hygiene: moisturize before swimming, rinse and dry thoroughly afterward, avoid sharing items, choose well-maintained pools, and treat minor skin injuries promptly. article.articleHeadline: ScienceNet: The mechanism governing replication efficiency of foot-and-mouth disease virus has been deciphered.
article.articleSummary: China's Lanzhou Veterinary Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, reports that host redox systems targeting the foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) RNA polymerase govern replication efficiency in animals. Using a pig genome-wide knockout library, researchers identified two host factors tightly linked to FMDV proliferation: methionine sulfoxide reductase B3 (MsrB3) and radical S-adenosylmethionine domain-containing protein 1 (RSAD1). The study shows these redox modulators regulate the stability and catalytic function of the viral RNA polymerase, directly determining the virus’s replication efficiency in pigs. This redox modification mechanism also modulates replication of multiple small RNA viruses. Published in Nature Communications, the work illuminates a refined virus–host interaction, uncovering key molecular targets and suggesting new avenues for broad-spectrum antiviral strategies against small RNA viruses.

article.articleHeadline: Review Highlights Evolving Pediatric Enterovirus Trends
article.articleSummary: Rapid enterovirus evolution—recombination is a core driver of diversity and antigenic change, hindering prevention and control. A Pediatric Investigation review (online 21 August 2026) details EV infections in children from hand-foot-and-mouth disease and herpangina to meningitis, hepatitis, pneumonia, and acute flaccid paralysis, with EV-D68 linked to AFM. Most infections are mild, but children under 5 are at higher risk due to immature immunity. Transmission occurs via fecal-oral routes and respiratory droplets, with asymptomatic carriers aiding spread. The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase lacks proofreading and recombination between serotypes accelerates genetic change; the C4 genotype of EV-A71 became predominant in China in 2004. Real-time RT-PCR remains the main diagnostic tool; treatment is supportive and no approved antivirals exist. Inactivated EV-A71 vaccines in China protect against EV-A71 but not CVA16/6/10, highlighting the need for multivalent vaccines plus hygiene, early diagnosis, isolation, and strengthened surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Summer outdoor activities: beware mosquitoes and other insects. Disease-control experts remind: in water, avoid 'hookworms'; on land, guard against 'vectors'.
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis risk dominates water play this summer as disease-control experts warn. Leptospira bacteria survive in warm, moist waters contaminated with animal urine, with mountain streams, ponds, ditches, and rice fields posing the highest source risk, especially after heavy rains or floods; seawater poses lower risk. Post-water fever with severe calf pain, red conjunctiva, and swollen lymph nodes warrants prompt medical evaluation, with a history of outdoor water exposure important for diagnosis. Do not self-medicate with NSAIDs or antibiotics before confirmation to avoid masking illness or triggering reactions. On land, Aedes albopictus mosquitoes—the primary dengue vector—breed in shaded, damp container habitats; avoid dengue-endemic areas. Other hazards include biting midges, centipedes, red fire ants, blister beetles, and venomous snakes. Wear protective clothing, camp in open, ventilated areas, and seek swift care if fever or joint pain and rash appear after outdoor activities.

article.articleSummary: Finland eases African swine fever (ASF) restrictions but expands restricted zones and tightens some controls. A possible second core area may form west of the zone as new data emerge. A new outer belt of 5–10 km would encircle the current zone, restricting only wild boar meat; hunters must submit samples from all wild boars shot in the belt. Outside the core, forestry and cultivation continue with limited rules; events up to 100 people and certain dog and hunting activities are allowed. Movement of farming/forestry machinery out of the zone requires cleaning/disinfection; exemptions can be granted via Ruokavirasto. A 500-euro per-sample bounty and a 500-euro report reward are introduced to boost hunting and reporting. Finland has ~600 pig farms, mainly in the Southwest/West; exports last year ~27 million kg (Korea, China, New Zealand, Japan, South Africa); Korea/NZ agreements exclude China/Japan, halting >€25 million in exports; compensation for ears/tails/snouts is being sought.

Yang Zhiyun says inclusion of first-line oral antivirals in medical insurance improves access; 2022 guidelines broadened eligibility for earlier intervention. article.articleHeadline: Dengue fever cases in Europe have tripled over the past decade; the EU seeks new lessons in mosquito prevention.
article.articleSummary: Europe's dengue fever cases have risen 300% from 2015 to 2024, with dengue, chikungunya, and West Nile fever spreading north as summers lengthen and winters warm. On 1 September 2026, EU's Florika Fink-Hooijer led a delegation to Singapore's National Environment Agency to study mosquito control through Wolbachia-infected male Aedes aegypti releases. The program expanded from five to 13 sites by 2022, and is projected to reach 800,000 households by year-end. A Nature Communications study estimated that without expansion dengue cases in 2023 would reach 13,748 in Singapore; actual reported were about 9,949, a ~28% reduction (~3,800 cases). Europe, where Aedes albopictus is the main vector, will adapt rather than copy Singapore's exact approach, leveraging European insect research collaborations.

These changes seek greater clinical relevance and cost allocation efficiency. Reported by CCTV News, reflecting ongoing public health financing reform in China.

article.articleHeadline: In another border region of Mongolia bordering Russia and China, activity of plague foci has been confirmed.
article.articleSummary: Active natural foci of bubonic plague were confirmed in Zavkhan Aimag, Mongolia, near the borders with Russia and China. Earlier reports show activity along the Russian border in Khövsgöl Aimag, with the region recording the last human death from plague in August 2025. In July 2026, laboratory confirmation of bubonic plague infection occurred in a patient from Hovd Aimag which borders China. A joint Russian–Mongolian monitoring program will run from 2026 to 2029. Approximately two-thirds of Mongolia lies within the transboundary Saylyugem plague focus; 1959–1990 monitoring linked circulating strains to Altai and, less commonly, Ulgei lineages. Risk exists in 83 soums across 15 aimags.

article.articleHeadline: 'It's in the realm of possibility': Climate change is spurring a reemergence of yellow fever, and the US could face future threats
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever, a mosquito-borne virus transmitted chiefly by Aedes aegypti, is reemerging in areas with little recent exposure as climate change expands mosquito ranges. The disease causes fever, muscle aches, headaches and vomiting; about 15% progress to severe illness with jaundice and bleeding, and severe cases have a 20–50% fatality rate. Globally, an estimated 31,000–82,000 deaths occur annually. Transmission typically starts from infected nonhuman primates to humans via mosquitoes, with urban outbreaks driven by Ae. aegypti in dense populations. Brazil’s 2017–2018 drought-linked outbreak centered on Belo Horizonte and São Paulo. Colombia’s Andes show reemergence after 1940 (preprint). Parts of Africa and South America previously low-risk are now seeing new outbreaks. In the U.S., Ae. aegypti already exists in Florida, Mississippi, Arizona and New Mexico, with models predicting northward expansion (Philadelphia, New York, Chicago by 2050) under warming. A 2017 WHO strategy seeks elimination of epidemics by 2026, underscoring vaccination as the key control.

article.articleHeadline: Warning over 'risky' meat imported from South American nation
article.articleSummary: UK farming unions urge a UK-wide ban on Brazilian meat after regulators found sex hormones and salmonella in Brazilian beef and chicken, warning of public health risk. May findings showed 80% of a frozen Brazilian chicken batch imported to Greece contained salmonella. Hormone oestrogen detected in Brazilian carcasses mixed into European beef shipments; EU and UK bans on such hormones cited. Brazil’s alleged failure to meet EU antibiotic-use limits fuels concerns about antimicrobial resistance. With the EU banning Brazilian meat from Thursday, UK ministers are urged to follow. UK imports of Brazilian poultry have risen to at least £5 billion since 2021, and 2024 Brazilian poultry accounted for about 13% of total UK chicken imports, much entering via food service with limited origin labeling. Separately, the UK salmonella outbreak has killed two and sickened 474, cases up 25% in a month, with eggs suspected; UKHSA investigating, risk considered low.

article.articleHeadline: With her daughter in the ICU and a severe viral infection, Juliano Cazarré's wife posts a powerful message: 'Supernatural' | Rádio Itatiaia
article.articleSummary: Maria Guilhermina, 4, daughter of Brazilian actor Juliano Cazarré and Letícia, remains in the Intensive Care Unit with a severe infection after an initial gastroenteritis progressed to pneumonia and a heavy infection. The child, who has Ebstein anomaly (a congenital heart defect), was admitted on Aug 30, 2026, with gastroenteritis; by Aug 31 the illness escalated to pneumonia and a serious infection. She required deep jugular venous access for medications due to fragile veins. Letícia, who herself had gastroenteritis and later norovirus, believes she transmitted the illness to her daughter. The mother, balancing work and hospital care, described strong faith and resilience amid the crisis. The case highlights pediatric infection in a child with complex cardiac history, underlining infection control and intensive care management in Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: Acre begins registering those affected by Hansen's disease for historical reparations.
article.articleSummary: Hansen’s disease (leprosy) in Acre, Brazil, prompts historical reparations as the state government begins registering individuals subjected to isolation and compulsory hospitalization through 1986. Under Law 3.407/2018, SEASDH will issue certificates recognizing the violations and offering apologies. Two registration teams operate: a mobile unit at the former Colônia Souza Araújo in Rio Branco’s Estrada Alberto Torres area, and a Morhan-led intake point in downtown Rio Branco. After document review to confirm eligibility, the first certificates are expected by September 21. The effort involves MPAC, TCE, PGE, DPE, SEASDH, and Sesacre, with plans for a permanent SEASDH reception point for applicants from other Acre municipalities. Morhan’s Bil Souza states the calendar aims to acknowledge and apologize for compulsory isolation and hospitalization up to 1986, including victims at Colônia Souza Araújo, Cruzeiro do Sul, and in seringais."

article.articleHeadline: Altered prions provoke severe decline in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
article.articleSummary: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a rare prion neurodegenerative disorder caused by misfolded prion protein in the brain, leading to rapid neurological decline. In Brazil, influencer Lito Sousa, 59, highlights progression with cognitive, behavioral, motor, coordination, and visual symptoms. Prions are brain proteins that, when misfolded, become resistant to proteases and propagate a chain reaction that damages neurons, causing a spongiform encephalopathy. Brazilian cases are mainly sporadic (about 85-90%), hereditary 5-15%, and acquired under 1% (iatrogenic) via procedures such as non-sterile deep brain electrodes, corneal transplants, growth hormone, liver transplants, neurosurgery, blood transfusions, or surgical instrumentation. Transmission is not via casual contact. There is no cure or disease-modifying treatment; care is supportive, and prion-targeted therapies are in clinical trials. Symptoms onset typically leads to death within months, underscoring diagnostic and management challenges in Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: Roraima conducts surveillance of backyard poultry to prevent avian influenza.
article.articleSummary: Roraima launches preventive surveillance for Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in backyard poultry across 11 rural properties. The action, coordinated by the Aderr Avian Health Program, collects blood and tracheal/cloacal swabs to monitor potential virus circulation near wild birds. Roraima has no registered HPAI outbreak, and current serology shows no suspicion or confirmation. Samples are processed locally at Lasan (Laboratório de Saúde Animal de Roraima) for serum separation and then sent to Campinas, São Paulo, at the MAPA laboratory for analysis and serology results. The initiative reinforces integration with national surveillance strategies to preserve the state's poultry health. Keepers are urged to report high mortality or unusual signs promptly to enable investigation and, if necessary, implement control measures. The surveillance emphasizes proactive prevention to safeguard Roraima’s aviculture status.

article.articleHeadline: HEOM creates tool to identify the risk of tuberculosis and anticipate isolation.
article.articleSummary: CT-TB Score, a chest CT-based risk score to identify patients at higher risk of tuberculosis and to anticipate isolation, was created from research conducted at Hospital Especializado Octávio Mangabeira (HEOM), a SESAB unit managed by Fundação José Silveira (FJS) in Brazil. The study, in collaboration with the FJS Center for Research, Learning and Innovation, evaluated 179 patients, including 74 with confirmed TB. It was presented at the 15th Paulista Infectology Congress. The proposed tool relies on imaging tests already available in routine hospital care, avoiding the need for new tests. By stratifying risk using existing CT data, it aims to support earlier isolation decisions and infection-control planning for suspected TB cases in hospital settings.

article.articleHeadline: São Carlos reaches 417 dengue fever cases
article.articleSummary: São Carlos, Brazil, as of September 1, 2026, records 417 confirmed dengue cases this year, with no dengue-related deaths. Despite the surge relative to prior years, this year’s figure reflects a dramatic drop from 19,641 confirmed cases in 2025 (~98% reduction). Notified cases total 3,397 in 2026, down from 26,581 in 2025 (87% decrease); notifications include positives, pending results, and discarded cases. The epidemiological bulletin also updates other mosquito-borne diseases: 203 discarded chikungunya cases, 189 discarded Zika cases, and 2 discarded yellow fever cases. The Epidemiological Surveillance emphasizes ongoing monitoring and reiterates the importance of vector control and personal precautions to prevent proliferation of Aedes aegypti and other arboviruses, despite substantial declines compared with 2025.

article.articleSummary: At a Brasília seminar, Brazil's Ministry of Health outlined strategies to strengthen national capacities and ensure sustainable SUS financing. Massuda traced federal health-budget trajectories, noting expansion resumed in 2023 and spending for 2023–2025 projected 26.2% above the pre-2023 period. He stressed constitutional resource earmarking and fiscal rules shaping expansion space. Discretionary resources increasingly flow through parliamentary amendments, which by 2025 total 47% of discretionary spending, underscoring the need for coordinating mechanisms to align investments with SUS priorities. The discussion urged pairing decentralization with national planning, regulation, provision of professionals, technology adoption, and strategic purchasing, citing Mais Médicos (about 27,000 professionals) strengthening Family Health teams. In specialized care, Teto MAC and Faec were highlighted; OCI would organize integrated care bundles, linking funding to outcomes and coordinating primary and specialized care. Centralized purchasing for medicines, vaccines, and high-cost technologies (e.g., Zolgensma, RSV vaccine) delivers savings and improved access. Massuda emphasized SUS sustainability.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola is back and the IMF's aid fund falls short
article.articleSummary: Ebola resurges in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) with over 2,000 confirmed deaths; UNDP warns the outbreak could push nearly a million people into poverty. The IMF’s debt relief mechanism for catastrophes, FFACC (originating from FFADC expansion after Ebola and COVID-19), is underfunded: FFACC resources total about $120 million, while DRC faces roughly $300 million in debt service in 2027 and cannot be supported single-handedly by existing funds. The article advocates selling a small, gradual fraction of the IMF’s gold reserves (about 90.5 million troy ounces; historical cost $45/oz; current market near $4,000/oz) to establish a permanent endowment to finance IMF concessional aid indefinitely. Donor contributions during COVID-19 (e.g., $800 million to the IMF; UK and Japan pledges) are insufficient long-term, highlighting the need to convert idle assets into a stable funding stream for crises.

article.articleHeadline: Hunting down the last cases of sleeping sickness
article.articleSummary: West African sleeping sickness (gambiense human African trypanosomiasis) persists in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with 471 cases reported worldwide in 2025, most in the DRC. WHO aims to eradicate transmission by 2030. EU-backed researchers lead the STROGHAT trial to test a simplified strategy using acoziborole, a single-dose oral drug endorsed by the EMA, in a country-wide effort to eliminate remaining cases. The parasite’s human reservoir and tsetse fly transmission cause fever, headaches, and joint pain; if untreated, it affects the brain and is almost always fatal. The screen-and-treat approach mobilizes teams to test villages; anyone with a positive screening test is treated immediately, while samples undergo laboratory confirmation. Acoziborole has shown 98.1% efficacy in trials, replacing older, toxic therapies like melarsoprol and reducing the need for invasive procedures in remote areas.

article.articleHeadline: DRC-Uganda: Easing of restrictive measures requested in response to Ebola for cross-border students - ACP
article.articleSummary: Kasindi, North Kivu, on the DRC-Uganda border, hosts a cross-border community seeking eased Ebola-related crossing restrictions for students who live in Uganda but study in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. As the 17th Ebola outbreak in Nord-Kivu and Ituri persists, Uganda has closed the Kasindi border. The start of the 2026–back-to-school season (Sept 1, 2026) heightens concern over schooling disruption. Fabrice Ndavo of COMESA urged special measures to allow two-country residents to cross safely, proposing coordinated controls and adherence to health measures, with schools, parents, and authorities jointly compiling a two-country list to facilitate access during border closures. The Nord-Kivu Ebola response bulletin reports 823 confirmed cases in the region, with eight new confirmations recorded in this outbreak. The request focuses on maintaining education continuity while sustaining infection-prevention protocols.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in North Kivu: Uganda funds the construction of a fourth treatment center in Butembo.
article.articleSummary: Ebola in North Kivu, DRC, advances as Uganda funds a fourth Ebola Treatment Center (ETC) in Butembo, a 60-bed facility at ITAV Kimemi. The center will include a lab able to diagnose Ebola virus disease and other illnesses in under four hours, with care by Congolese and Ugandan specialists. A delegation led by the North Kivu liaison chief, the zone medical chief, and Deputy Jeannine Kavira Katasohire visited on August 31 to assess progress. The deputy urged residents to stay vigilant, follow prevention measures, cooperate with health teams, and protect response infrastructure from stigma. Uganda expressed solidarity with Congo’s outbreak response; it recently ended a Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak. Butembo is the province’s hotspot: as of August 30, 2026, Nord-Kivu had 823 confirmed cases and 574 deaths, with 540 in Butembo. A Matanda ETC will open soon, bringing four ETCs in Butembo alongside Katwa and Kitatumba. Uganda had deployed about 50 experts to the region.

article.articleHeadline: Comoros | Cholera - Simplified Early Action Protocol Activation (sEAP №: MDRKM015 | sEAP2023KM02) - Comoros
article.articleSummary: Cholera is the prioritized hazard for Comoros’s sEAP2023KM02. Comoros is not endemic but highly connected to East/Central Africa, with recurrent outbreaks in Tanzania, Mozambique, Kenya, DRC, Rwanda, Burundi, and Ethiopia. From December 2024 through January 2026, these countries reported 101,351 cases and 2,452 deaths; Kenya and Rwanda outbreaks ended in 2025, while others remained active through January 2026. Climate risks—sea-level rise, storm surges, flooding, heat—and limited services amplify transmission, especially during Nov–May rains. Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, and cramps with rapid dehydration. Importation from neighboring countries and mass gatherings such as Grand Weddings drive risk in Comoros. Since 1975, >29,000 cases and 672 deaths (CFR ~3.16%). The 2024 outbreak linked to a boat from Tanzania peaked at 11,171 cases and 153 deaths; children under 15 accounted for >35% of cases and 67% of deaths.

article.articleHeadline: A fly carrying more than 100 pathogens could bring disease to your dinner plate.
article.articleSummary: Houseflies (Musca domestica) can carry more than 130 pathogens across 21 countries, primarily bacteria such as Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Shigella, Campylobacter, and Listeria, with viruses, fungi and parasites also reported. A notable experimental study shows E. coli on a fly can transfer to a clean surface after a single landing, illustrating mechanical transmission from contaminated sources to food or surfaces. Actual risk depends on pathogen type, load, prior exposure, and food type. While not every fly carries disease, higher risk occurs in crowded, unsanitary settings near livestock or waste. Preventive measures include covering food outdoors, proper storage, kitchen cleanliness, regular waste disposal, and separating raw and cooked foods. CDC recommends core food-safety practices: clean, separate, cook thoroughly, and refrigerate; discard foods left open with many flies.

article.articleHeadline: Five Common Misconceptions About Meningococcal Disease
article.articleSummary: Five common misconceptions about meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) addressed by Ho Chi Minh City's Department of Preventive Medicine (HCDC). Misconception 1: it only affects young children. Reality: it can occur at any age; teens, young adults, dorm residents, military personnel, and immunocompromised individuals are at risk. Misconception 2: contact with an infected person guarantees infection. Transmission is via respiratory droplets or saliva during close or prolonged exposure; risk depends on exposure level and immune status; close contacts may receive prophylaxis as needed. Misconception 3: it only causes meningitis. The bacteria can cause bacteremia/septicemia, a rapid, life-threatening illness; symptoms include sudden high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, rash, nausea/vomiting, or confusion, requiring urgent care. Misconception 4: one vaccine dose provides lifelong protection. Protection can wane; boosters may be needed depending on vaccine type, age, and risk. Misconception 5: healthy people cannot get meningococcal disease. Carriers can transmit without symptoms; prevention includes vaccination as indicated, hand hygiene, covering coughs, ventilation, and avoiding close contact with suspected cases. HCDC urges timely medical evaluation for suspected cases and high-risk individuals.

article.articleHeadline: UPSC Mains Answer Practice -- GS 3: Himalayan region's natural hazards and typhoid control in India (Week 170)
article.articleSummary: As of 1 September 2026, UPSC Essentials’ Week 170 practice highlights two themes: Himalayan natural hazards and typhoid control in India. Question 2 cites the statement 'The control of vaccine-preventable diseases cannot rely primarily on treatment' in the typhoid context. The Himalayan region faces cascading hazards from glacial processes, steep terrain, and extreme weather, with factors such as glacier retreat, formation of glacial lakes, GLOFs, landslides, and debris flows; past incidents Kedarnath (2013), Chamoli (2021), and South Lhonak (2023) illustrate the cascade. Climate change and rapid infrastructure—hydroelectric projects, tunneling, highways, and dense tourism—heighten vulnerability, especially along narrow river valleys. Measures proposed: enhanced monitoring of glacial lakes, landslides, and river flows using weather stations, river gauges, satellites, and environmental seismology; restrict development in hazard zones; require cumulative, multi-hazard risk assessments for dams and roads; develop evacuation plans, early warning, and cross-border data exchange among India, Nepal, Bhutan, and China.

article.articleSummary: During the monsoon in Delhi, the risk of Hepatitis A rises due to contaminated water, flooding, and spoiled food spreading the virus. At Delhi's RML Hospital, Dr. Subhash Giri notes rising Hepatitis A cases. Early symptoms include fever, fatigue, reduced appetite, and abdominal pain or diarrhea; jaundice may develop later. Diagnosis is confirmed by blood tests. There is no specific antiviral therapy; most patients recover with rest, adequate fluids, and proper nutrition, but untreated infection can lead to liver failure. Prevention focuses on boiling drinking water, handwashing, and safe food handling. Seek urgent care if severe abdominal pain with fever and vomiting or signs of jaundice appear.

article.articleHeadline: WHO revises typhoid vaccine advice
article.articleSummary: India’s 2023 typhoid burden: about 4.9 million cases, 7.3 lakh hospitalisations, and 7,850 deaths (Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia). Of hospitalisations, 82% involved fluoroquinolone-resistant typhoid, with roughly 6 lakh admissions tied to drug resistance. Children drive the burden: 5–9 years 36%, 10–14 years 27%, 6 months–4 years 25%. Amid rising antimicrobial resistance, including reports of carbapenem-resistant Salmonella Typhi, WHO updated guidance on typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV). First dose at 9–24 months in high-incidence settings; India could align with the 18‑month visit to give TCV with the second measles dose, with single-dose impact likely. A school-entry booster could be considered in high-burden urban areas if protection wanes; boosters around five years may be advised in very high-incidence settings. Vaccination complements, not replaces, basic measures (WASH, safe water, sanitation, hygiene) and timely diagnosis/treatment. NTAGI recommended including TCV in India’s Universal Immunisation Programme in 2022.

article.articleHeadline: Water accumulated around the home during the monsoon can cause dengue and malaria; prevent mosquito breeding with these simple measures.
article.articleSummary: Monsoon water around homes in India can drive dengue and malaria outbreaks as Aedes mosquitoes breed in small amounts of clean standing water in household containers. Common sites include roof gutters, balconies, plant pots and plates, coolers, buckets, old tires, and other items where water can stagnate for a few days. Exposure on rooftops or while tending plants after rain can lead to bites, so prevention must go beyond staying indoors. Weekly cleaning is essential: completely empty, scrub, and dry containers rather than just pouring out water to remove eggs. Regularly inspect roofs, balconies, and drainage to prevent stagnation. Ensure coolers do not hold water when not in use, and avoid overwatering plants or leaving water in plant trays. Protective habits—long sleeves, screens, and mosquito repellents—help reduce risk of dengue and malaria starting at home.

article.articleHeadline: H1N1 Is Surging In India. So Why Are So Few People Getting The Flu Shot?
article.articleSummary: H1N1 is surging in India as seasonal influenza activity rises, yet flu vaccination remains far from routine for most of the population. The Union Health Ministry said in August that the H1N1 viruses circulating in India align with typical seasonal patterns observed in recent years, with no new or unusually dangerous strain detected. Genetic surveillance shows only small genetic changes consistent with normal influenza evolution. While this means there is no emerging pandemic, seasonal influenza is not harmless and can cause significant illness. Vaccination demand is growing but uptake remains limited, contributing to vulnerability as cases rise. The situation highlights the gap between widespread disease activity and vaccine coverage, with India monitoring circulating strains and encouraging vaccine use to mitigate potential morbidity and mortality from H1N1 during the ongoing seasonal wave.

article.articleHeadline: Rising HIV cases in Sheikhpura spark panic: 30 new patients in eight months; including three inmates from the jail
article.articleSummary: HIV infections are rising in Sheikhpura district, triggering public health action. In eight months, 30 new HIV cases have been identified, including three inmates from Sheikhpura jail. About 500 people are already living with HIV and receiving treatment. New infections include a couple, a pregnant woman, an unborn baby, and an unmarried young man, indicating ongoing transmission. The health department plans confidentially identifying high-risk areas for targeted testing, counseling, and awareness campaigns to curb spread. A review of the AIDS control program was led by the Deputy Commissioner, who mandated expanded identification, testing, treatment, and prevention efforts. A two-month awareness drive will run through October, with camps in schools, colleges, and local neighborhoods to educate on HIV causes, prevention, testing, and treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Delhi man makes full recovery in over 2 years; survives six surgeries, rare skull bone TB
article.articleSummary: New Delhi, 53-year-old man admitted to Fortis Hospital, Shalimar Bagh, after a brain hemorrhage left him semi-comatose. Emergency decompressive craniectomy and temporary skull opening were followed by prolonged ventilator support and a tracheostomy, with intensive care for nearly a month before regaining consciousness. He later required repeated brain surgery for seizures and a clot beneath the replaced skull, and his own skull bone preserved in a bone bank was used for re-implantation. Months later a discharge from the surgical wound prompted investigations that diagnosed tuberculosis of the skull bone, an exceptionally uncommon post-brain-surgery complication. The infected bone was removed, and prolonged anti-tuberculosis therapy was started; TB involving brain and spine was also identified. He endured repeated neurological weakness, infections, and a thigh-bone fracture, ultimately reconstructed with a custom PEEK cranial implant and partial vision loss from optic neuritis. By 2026-09-02, he returned to independent life after two-and-a-half years of multidisciplinary care.

article.articleHeadline: NIT will develop an effective treatment system for Legionella infection.
article.articleSummary: National Institute of Technology (NIT) Jamshedpur, through its Department of Chemistry, is launching a Department of Science and Technology (DST)-funded project on Legionella infection. Guided by Dr. Puja Kumari, the study aims to understand the infection mechanism at the molecular level, specifically how human E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme interacts with bacterial proteins released during Legionella entry into host cells. By elucidating these protein-protein interactions, researchers seek to uncover how Legionella hijacks the host cellular machinery. The ultimate goal is to translate mechanistic insights into the development of effective therapeutic measures against Legionella infection in the future. The project reflects ongoing scientific efforts in Jamshedpur as of 1 September 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Mosquito menace worsens as monsoon breeds dengue fear
article.articleSummary: Hyderabad’s Cyberabad (CMC) and Malkajgiri (MMC) limits face intensified mosquito menace during the monsoon, heightening dengue risk from Aedes aegypti and malaria concerns. Hotspots include Manikonda area — Kohinoor Enclave, Alkapur Road — and water-logged sites near Ibrahimbagh Lake, Pandenavagu Nala, and EVV Colony. Authorities launched a major mosquito-control push in April with 10 EV-based fogging machines (followed by eight more); each unit covers about 150 km per operation and runs for over six hours. Yet residents in Yapral, Nagaram, Kapra, Safilguda, Moula Ali, Nacharam, Mirzalguda and Cherlapally report irregular fogging and demand interior-area coverage, source elimination, drain cleaning, and regular anti-larval actions. MMC cites ~18 EV fogging machines and evening operations, with dedicated teams for hotspots and calls for ward-wise fogging schedules and monitoring to curb potential dengue outbreaks.

article.articleHeadline: West Aceh Health Office Continues to Provide Treatment for 237 Tuberculosis Patients.
article.articleSummary: West Aceh Regency Health Office continues treatment for 237 tuberculosis (TB) patients across several subdistricts. Health Chief Evi Darni told ANTARA in Meulaboh that care supports cure for detected cases. The regency provides medical accompaniment and nutrition aid, with Puskesmas clients receiving high-protein, high-calorie foods such as milk and mung beans regularly. To boost screening participation, transport subsidies of Rp30,000 per village are provided, with a target of 100 people per screening point. Patients must adhere to a regimen: daily medicines for the first three months, then twice weekly for months four to six; after six months, re-evaluation. If bacteria persist, treatment can extend by three more months to nine months total. Long-term efforts include ongoing TB prevention campaigns via social media and community activities.

article.articleHeadline: Beware Monkeypox, East Java Quarantine Office Tightens Surveillance of Monkey Traffic.
article.articleSummary: East Java's Animal, Fish, and Plant Quarantine Office tightens surveillance of monkey traffic at 27 entry/exit points in Jawa Timur to curb disease risk from primates. The intensified checks cover monkeys imported, exported, or moved domestically within Indonesia. Plt Kepala Karantina Jatim Hudiansyah Is Nursal says the aim is to ensure animals are healthy and not disease vectors. Under Indonesian quarantine decision 2664/2025, primates warrant heightened attention due to potential to carry diseases transmissible to humans (zoonoses). Diseases of concern include rabies, listeriosis, hepatitis B, HIV, flavivirus infections, leishmaniasis, Marburg, yellow fever, monkeypox, and Zika. Vendors and individuals must provide SATS-DN/LN documents, CITES when required, and a negative rabies test with clinical examinations. Physical inspection and quarantine are mandatory to prevent zoonotic transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Taiwan reports more dengue in Kaohsiung City
article.articleSummary: As of 1 September 2026, Taiwan CDC reports three new locally transmitted dengue cases in Kaohsiung City from a family cluster. The index case, a man in his 60s from Gangshan District, developed fever, muscle and joint pain, and nausea on 26 August; dengue virus type 2 was confirmed and he plus two of five cohabitants were hospitalized. No overseas travel during the incubation period, indicating local transmission near home. Nationwide, 145 dengue cases have been confirmed in 2026: 10 locally acquired (all in Kaohsiung) and 135 imported, led by Vietnam (28), Indonesia (27), and the Maldives (16). The total is below 2025’s 154. Authorities expanded epidemiological investigations, increased mosquito density surveys, and surrounding-area measures including breeding-ground elimination and health education. Prevention: home inspections, post-rain checks, light clothing, DEET/Picaridin/IR-3535 repellents; seek care for dengue-like symptoms and report travel history; TOCC inquiries emphasized for clinicians.

The university said she was accompanied by family, department, and study program during hospitalization. Her body was taken to Serang, Banten for the family’s rites. An official report from the Faculty of Medicine confirms she was indeed an FK Undip student. The report attributes death to dengue fever; there is no factual basis for the bullying claim.

article.articleHeadline: Singapore Influenza Surge: Cases Rise Sharply but Infections Not More Severe Than Usual - Best Breaking News and Beyond: Singapore, Batam and some say JB
article.articleSummary: Singapore reports a notable rise in influenza activity, with influenza-like illness positivity up to 36.6% in Aug 16–22, from 24.0% previously. Infectious diseases specialist Leong Hoe Nam identifies H3N2 as the circulating strain. The Communicable Diseases Agency (CDA) says there is currently no evidence that infections are more severe than typical seasonal flu, and it continues monitoring. Seasonal influenza activity typically peaks May–Aug and Dec–Mar. Vaccination is recommended for high-risk groups: children 6 months–4 years, adults 65+, pregnant women, and those with certain chronic conditions. Public guidance includes staying home with mild respiratory symptoms, wearing a mask if going out, minimizing social contact, avoiding crowded places, and seeking medical care if symptoms worsen or in high-risk individuals. Ongoing monitoring is important given frequent travel between Singapore and neighboring regions, including Batam and the Riau Islands.

article.articleHeadline: Only 48.6% of TB cases detected, Gianyar Regency Health Office, Bali forms TB Task Force.

At the grassroots level, the district directs all villages to establish TB Alert Villages no later than 30 September 2026. The region also drafted a Regional Action Plan for TB control toward the national TB elimination target by 2030, emphasizing shared responsibility.

article.articleHeadline: Babel quarantine rejects undocumented chickens to prevent avian flu.
article.articleSummary: Three chickens were refused entry at Pangkalpinang's Depati Amir Airport by Indonesia's Quarantine Agency (Barantan) via the Bangka Belitung Islands Animal, Fish, and Plant Quarantine Center, due to lack of a health quarantine certificate from the origin. On 1 September 2026, inspectors found no accompanying health certificate during administrative checks, prompting a rejection to prevent potential avian influenza (AI) spread. Quarantine chief Herwintarti said even a small number of birds can serve as disease vectors, underscoring biosecurity at entry points. The incident illustrates enforcement of cross-border animal movement rules under Law No. 21/2019 on Quarantine of Animals, Fish, and Plants, and the need for proper health documentation for any inter-regional transport of animals, fish, or plants. Public urged to verify quarantine requirements before transporting or shipping goods.

article.articleHeadline: Kpone Kokompe records four confirmed measles cases
article.articleSummary: Four confirmed measles cases have been reported in Kpone Kokompe, Kpone-Katamanso Municipality. Health authorities, led by Medical Superintendent Dr. Jemima Quarte Mensah of Kpone District Hospital, intensified surveillance and contact tracing to contain the outbreak and prevent further spread. During the Kpone-Katamanso Municipal Assembly General Assembly, she said contact tracing and planned activities had been successfully undertaken to contain and eradicate the infection in the community. Parents and guardians were urged to report suspected cases promptly to nearest health facilities for investigation and management, and to avoid traditional remedies or unapproved treatments, as self-medication could worsen outcomes or cause preventable deaths. Institutions with large gatherings—churches and schools—were urged to reinforce hygiene, monitor for illness, and encourage prompt medical attention. Community cooperation and early reporting were emphasized to prevent spread to other communities within the municipality.

article.articleHeadline: Airport malaria in Frankfurt: How big is the danger?
article.articleSummary: Six Frankfurt Airport employees were infected with malaria by an imported Anopheles mosquito, with two deaths. The Health Department is tracing the mosquito source; blood tests may reveal whether a single mosquito bit multiple people and the origin. Antwerp's Institute of Tropical Medicine is analyzing samples, with results expected in six to eight weeks. A 2022 incident at the same airport involved three workers and suggested a single mosquito, possibly from Ghana, arrived via layover since there were no direct flights from Ghana to the Rhine-Main region at the time. Malaria in Germany is rare; Anopheles mosquitos there do not carry the parasite unless previously infected, and past infections occurred in summer months. Malaria tropica is most dangerous for those without prior exposure. Experts say true protection comes from eradicating the parasite in origin countries; imported cases reduce risk.

article.articleHeadline: Philippines tallies nearly 118,000 dengue cases
article.articleSummary: As of September 1, 2026, the Philippines has recorded 117,952 dengue cases from January–August 2026, per the Department of Health (DOH). The figure is about 41% lower than 201,533 cases reported last year. Officials warn cases may spike in the coming weeks with the ongoing rainy season and stagnant water that fosters mosquito breeding. Water sources include buckets, drums, flowerpots, gutters, canals, tires, cans, jars, and bottles. Dengue is an acute viral infection transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Symptoms include high fever, joint and muscle pain, pain behind the eyes, weakness, skin rashes, nosebleeds as fever subsides, abdominal pain, vomiting coffee-colored material, dark stools, and breathing difficulties. The DOH advises protective measures: wear clothing covering the skin, use mosquito repellent, and avoid areas with many mosquitoes. Communities should clean surroundings and remove standing water, practicing tip over, shake, dry, and cover to prevent mosquito proliferation.

article.articleHeadline: Bogotá and PAHO sign an alliance to eliminate transmissible diseases.
article.articleSummary: Bogotá, in partnership with PAHO/WHO Colombia, launched the Plan District to Accelerate the Elimination of Transmissible Diseases, targeting by 2030 six priority diseases: tuberculosis, leprosy, congenital syphilis, mother-to-child transmission of HIV, measles and rubella, and dog-transmitted human rabies. The initiative accompanies the opening of Suba’s tenth Specialized Resolutive Service (SER Suba), within the Subred Norte network, to bring high-resolutive ambulatory care closer to residents (population 48,612). The plan is integrated with Hospital Fray Bartolomé de las Casas and Hospital de Suba, aiming to shorten delays and improve timely diagnoses. Demographics show a large share of adults and seniors served (42% adults, 18% seniors). Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading mortality cause in Bogotá’s 30–70-year-olds, with 2010–2025 deaths totaling 36,545 (about 45.3% of noncommunicable deaths in this group). No outbreak counts are provided.

article.articleHeadline: Get well soon! 'Noey Waruttha' wants to be sick instead of her child 'Little Keith' contracting COVID.
article.articleSummary: Thai mother Noey Waruttha Imraporn revealed on August 31 via Instagram that her son Keith (Nong Keith) has contracted COVID-19—the first illness of his life—and was hospitalized. Keith underwent a blood draw, received bitter medicine, and was connected to an IV drip, while medical staff monitored his temperature, wiped him down, and suctioned nasal mucus. The post describes Keith crying and Noey’s wish to be sick instead of him, expressing profound parental concern. She praised the doctors and nurses for the care Keith received during his hospital stay. article.articleHeadline: Thailand Sees COVID-19 Surge as Fatality Rates Hit Record Low
article.articleSummary: Thailand reports a COVID-19 surge during the 2026 rainy season, with 99,691 cases recorded January 1–August 31 (about 151.34 per 100,000) and 15 deaths, for a case fatality rate of 0.02%. Illness remains generally mild, with most patients experiencing upper respiratory symptoms and recovering at home; hospital and ICU demand remains within normal capacity. Officials credit high vaccination coverage, prior exposures, and early outpatient therapies for limiting severity. The surge coincides with monsoon indoor crowding and humidity, with concurrent spikes of seasonal influenza and RSV across several provinces. Protecting vulnerable groups— seniors, pregnant women, and those with chronic conditions—through boosters and preventive measures is advised. Free screening and antivirals are available at public facilities. No domestic travel restrictions; international tourism continues. Weekly public updates are planned as the rainy season winds down.

article.articleHeadline: Ministry of Public Health steps up monkeypox surveillance after surge in cases, says Clade Ib strain accounts for the majority and symptoms are more severe than before.
article.articleSummary: Thailand reports 254 confirmed mpox cases from January 1 to August 23, 2026, with Clade Ib accounting for 193 cases and Clade II for 58; three cases await subtype confirmation. Clade Ib is associated with more severe symptoms and lesions, especially among immunocompromised individuals. Most cases are in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region, other large cities, and tourist provinces. Primary risk factors remain close contact related to sexual activity and use of closed or crowded venues. Mpox transmits via direct contact with skin lesions, body fluids, or prolonged close contact. The Department of Disease Control has stepped up surveillance and integrated screening with STI and HIV clinics, and reinforced infection-control measures in health facilities, with a nationwide helpline at 1422. Public guidance urges personal hygiene, avoiding contact with people with abnormal skin, and seeking medical care within 5–21 days after exposure if fever, headache, myalgia, lymphadenopathy, or rash develops.

article.articleHeadline: Botswana Races to Protect Beef Exports as FMD Outbreak Shuts EU Fresh-Beef Market
article.articleSummary: Botswana tightens cattle movements to contain foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) and restore export access after EU suspensions in 2026. Agriculture Minister said 54 cattle entered an FMD containment zone in Metlobo. EU restrictions began in Maitengwe in February and, after an April Southern District outbreak, expanded to all Botswana zones still allowed to export fresh meat. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) suspended FMD‑free status for several Botswana zones. EU rules restrict movement between zones with different disease statuses. Beef exports via the Botswana Meat Commission totaled about P2.36 billion (2020–2025); meat exports were P404 million in 2024 and P312 million in 2023, while live cattle exports were P523 million (2024) and P648 million (2023). SAT 1 serotype is present in Southern Africa, with outbreaks in Lesotho, Eswatini, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Agriculture accounted for about 1.7% of GDP in 2023 and agricultural exports 1.1% of total in 2024.
